sharedText: they suffered themselves to be slain according to the desires of their enemies
reason: The scene is the KJV's chief image of unresisted death — 'he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter' — and a reader who has just come from Alma 24's mass martyrdom will hear it. But Alma 27:3 has no lamb, no sheep, no silence and no shearers, and 'suffered themselves to be slain' is the Book of Mormon's own construction, used of this people four times in three chapters. Isaiah 53 is heavily worked elsewhere in the book (Mosiah 14 transcribes it) and this catalogue records dependence, not resemblance. The typology is real and the wording will not carry it.

sharedText: as though they were angels sent from God
reason: 'Sent from God' occurs in two KJV verses, John 1:6 ('there was a man sent from God, whose name was John') and Luke 1:26 ('the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee'), and Luke 1:26 has the angel as well, which makes it look decisive. It is not: 'sent from God' is three ordinary words of which the Book of Mormon uses two dozen variants, and neither KJV verse has anyone treated AS THOUGH he were an angel, which is the whole content of the clause. The verse's identifiable borrowing is 'moved with compassion', filed as a link against Matthew 9:36.

sharedText: desiring the voice of the people
reason: 'The voice of the people' is adjudicated at Mosiah 7:9 against 1 Samuel 8:7 — Israel's demand for a king — and again at Mosiah 29:2 and Alma 2:7, where the phrase returns to the passage it first translated because the institution being described is the one Mosiah put in the king's place. Alma 27:21 is that institution running normally: the chief judge sends a proclamation and the voice of the people answers. Registered here rather than passed over because of what the answer is. 1 Samuel 8:7's voice of the people rejects the LORD from reigning over them; Alma 27:22's voice of the people gives away a province to a foreign people that has been trying to kill them, and pays for an army to defend it. That is the sharpest contrast the phrase has been put to in the book, and it is an argument for the institution rather than a fresh borrowing. A reader should be sent to Mosiah 7:9 and Alma 2:7.

sharedText: they were perfectly honest and upright in all things
reason: Tempting and just short. 'Perfect and upright' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 1:1 — 'that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil' — repeated by the LORD at 1:8 and 2:3, and it is the KJV's formal character-summary, which is the genre of Alma 27:27. But the Book of Mormon's words are 'perfectly honest and upright', with an adverb and an added noun, and 'honest' is not in Job's formula at any point. The pair 'perfect and upright' is not reproduced. The verse's two identifiable borrowings, Acts 22:3 and Hebrews 3:6, are filed as links; this clause between them is the one the KJV does not account for.

sharedText: death was swallowed up to them by the victory of Christ over it
reason: This is 1 Corinthians 15:54's 'Death is swallowed up in victory' and it is not in doubt; it is adjudicated at Alma 22:14, where Aaron's preaching to the Lamanite king brings four of Paul's terms together in one clause and the row stands at 'certain'. Alma 27:28 is the fruit of that sermon reported in the sermon's own words — the same people, five chapters later, no longer fearing death — so it is a recurrence rather than a fresh borrowing, and the register should send a reader to 22:14. Note that the chapter uses Paul's verb twice: at 27:17 it is joy that swallows a man up, which is filed as a link against 2 Corinthians 2:7, the KJV's one verse for a person swallowed up with a feeling.

sharedText: a highly favored people of the Lord
reason: 'Highly favoured' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Gabriel's salutation to Mary at Luke 1:28, and it was adjudicated for this book at Alma 13:23, with an earlier row at Mosiah 1:13. (The Book of Mormon's opening sentence, 1 Nephi 1:1's 'having been born of goodly parents … highly favored of the Lord', carries no row for the phrase in this catalogue; the pilot adjudicated that verse against Exodus 2:2 on 'goodly' alone.) By Alma 27:30 it is the book's standing epithet for a people under divine favour and no longer a fresh borrowing. Worth the entry for the trajectory: a phrase the KJV uses once, of one woman, at an annunciation, becomes in the Book of Mormon a collective political status, and 27:30 applies it to a people that six chapters ago was outside the covenant altogether.
